idiom_name: #private field + typed guard methods; Proxy-based transparent guard behind an interface
implementation_notes: TypeScript's own private/protected modifiers are type-system-only - 'Like other aspects of TypeScript's type system, private and protected are only enforced during type checking' - so bracket notation and runtime lookups still reach the member and the modifier disappears from the emitted JavaScript; a TS-only caller is constrained, a JS caller or an as-any cast is not. The realization that survives compilation is the #private field, which is 'hard private': it remains private after compilation and has no bracket-notation escape, with the compiler caveat that targets below ES2022 emit WeakMap-based privacy (still private, different mechanism). The guard is therefore a class with a #resource plus public methods that check the policy first, exposed behind an interface so callers depend on the narrow contract; where the resource's existing API must stay usable, the JavaScript Proxy in typed form provides transparent interception. Structural typing is a separate trap on the type side: conforming to the interface does not prove the runtime object is the guard, so the guard must be the only constructor of the value in practice.
pitfalls: private/protected/readonly are erased at runtime and enforced only by the type checker ('soft private': bracket notation is checked and allowed for private) - only # fields are private after compilation.

Structural typing means any object of the right shape satisfies the interface; a public constructor or a factory that accepts a pre-built store lets callers substitute their own object, so the guard must own construction.
Downlevel emits (ES2021 and below) implement # fields with WeakMaps: privacy still holds, but debugging output differs, and code that copies own properties silently loses them.
A Proxy-based guard is invisible to the type system: type callers against the interface, keep the target out of shared structures, and remember instanceof/identity checks see the proxy.

variants.name: Typed Proxy trap guard (transparent, revocable)
variants.implementation_notes: For callers that must keep using the resource's own interface, the guard is a typed handler over a Proxy: ProxyHandler<T> types the traps, each trap consults the policy and forwards with Reflect so internal-method semantics stay intact, and the target is captured in the closure rather than exposed on the guard. The type parameter documents which interface callers see, while the runtime guard - not the type - performs the check; Proxy.revocable() adds revoke(), the typed analogue of withdrawing a capability. Choose it when rewriting callers onto a narrower interface is not an option; the costs are identity surprises and the fact that the type system cannot express 'the target is private'.
pitfalls: The handler and the target must stay out of the returned object: exposing either (or a closure that returns the target) hands callers the resource the proxy was supposed to own.
Trap invariants are runtime-checked: a trap that reports a non-configurable property differently (or violates [[GetPrototypeOf]] on an extensible target) throws a TypeError.
revoke() only invalidates the proxy; calls that already captured the target continue, so revocation semantics belong in the policy object, not in the revoke call alone.
